newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran at crossroads in presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Iran at crossroads in presidential poll.

text.p: Iran is in the throes of the most keenly fought election in the 18 years of its Islamic revolution.
At stake in Friday's poll is the direction the Islamic republic of 60 million people should take in economic development.

For the first time since Shi'ite Moslem mullahs overthrew the autocratic Shah in 1979, Iranians have a choice of which way to go: down a conservative road likely to reverse some of President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's market reforms or along a new route offering alternative solutions to the dilemma of how to reconcile economic change with demands for social justice.

Although the clergy-dominated government has recently won praise from the International Monetary Fund for reviving growth and curbing inflation, the economy -- marred by soaring prices and insufficient jobs -- is the primary campaign issue.
There will be no shift in Iran's foreign policy stance when Rafsanjani steps down in August, Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Sunday.
Tehran's diplomatic agenda and relations with the rest of the world are determined by the supreme leader and paramount authority Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, whose word is sacrosanct.
Khamenei, successor to the revolution's leading spiritual light the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, is responsible for executing God's will according to divine law.
He is also commander-in-chief of Iran's battle-hardened armed forces of more than half-a-million men.
In a recent radio broadcast the Ayatollah said Iranians would never vote for any candidate who was soft on the West or for "foreign political and cultural aggression".

Officials have told independent Western analysts in Tehran that it did not matter which of the two election front-runners - - Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri and Mohammad Khatami -- won because Khamenei determines the overall foreign policy and direction.
And Velayati told a news conference on Sunday there would be no change in the principles of Iran's foreign policy.

But there could be a difference in style. Nateq-Nouri, the 54-year-old speaker of the Majlis (parliament) renowned for his conservatism and anti-Western views, is ahead in the only opinion poll published thus far.

He has been backed by key clerical groups and is close to the bazaaris, traders who make up Iran's merchant class and who fear their traditional economic and political advantage are threatened by foreign investment in the economy.
The conservative deputies he leads have slowed Rafsanjani's market reforms but Nateq-Nouri's supporters now say he would push ahead with them if elected.

Khatami, also 54, is a left-leaning ex-culture and Islamic guidance minister who advocates less heavy-handed social and cultural rules and policies. He is known to favour open debate on sensitive topics like attitudes towards the West.
A descendant of Islam's founder Prophet Mohammad, he is backed by a coalition of centrists and technocrats close to Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views.
The other two candidates -- Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri and Reza Zaverei -- are rated outsiders.

No change in foreign policy means no change in the standoff between Iran and the European Union over a German court verdict accusing Iran's leaders of involvement in the killings of three Kurdish dissidents and their translator in Berlin.
The charge, vehemently denied in Iran, raised tempers and flared into an ugly long-distance slanging match last month between Tehran and European capitals.
Velayati said it was up to the Berlin court to "rectify" its position.

Iran's other foreign policy priorities include carving out a zone of influence in Central Asia and the Caucasus, looking east to Asia for trade, and trying to get on better terms with Iran's neighbours to the south, where the oil-rich Gulf Arabs of Saudi Arabia and its allies are suspicious of Iranian overtures and intentions.

But any initiative for some sort of relationship with the United States, despite calls from Washington foreign policy think-tanks for a review of the Clinton administration's strategy of isolating Iran, is unlikely to come from Tehran.

The United States, which has had no ties with Iran since 1980 at the height of the American embassy hostage crisis, remains the "Great Satan" in the religious leadership's demonology and its avowed arch-enemy.
